plain_english: None of these writers will force you to die, but all of them will teach you how to live well. None will waste your time — they'll add their own lifetimes to yours. Their conversations aren't dangerous. Their friendship won't get you executed. Their company won't bankrupt you. You can take whatever you want from them. They won't stop you from drinking deeply from their wisdom. What happiness awaits someone who makes these great minds his guides! He'll have friends to discuss everything with, big and small. He can ask their advice every day. They'll tell him the truth without being cruel. They'll praise him without flattery. And he can shape his own character based on their example.
original_excerpt: None of these men will force you to die, but all of them will teach you how to die: none of these will waste your time, but will add his own to it. The talk of these men is not dangerous, their friendship will not lead you to the scaffold, their society will not ruin you in expenses: you may take from them whatsoever you will; they will not prevent your taking the deepest draughts of their wisdom that you please. What blessedness, what a fair old age awaits the man who takes these for his patrons! he will have friends with whom he may discuss all matters, great and small, whose advice he may ask daily about himself, from whom he will hear truth without insult, praise without flattery, and according to whose likeness he may model his own character.
source_reference: On the Shortness of Life, Section 15

plain_english: We usually say we can't choose our parents — that we're stuck with whoever chance gave us. But we can choose to be born into any intellectual family we want. There are many noble minds to pick from. Choose which one you'd like to belong to. When you adopt their ideas, you don't just get their name. You also get their wealth of wisdom. And this wealth isn't meant to be hoarded like a miser guards his coins. The more people you share it with, the richer it becomes. These great thinkers will show you the path to immortality. They'll lift you to heights where no one can knock you down.
original_excerpt: We are wont to say that we are not able to choose who our parents should be, but that they were assigned to us by chance; yet we may be born just as we please: there are several families of the noblest intellects: choose which you would like to belong to: by your adoption you will not receive their name only, but also their property, which is not intended to be guarded in a mean and miserly spirit: the more persons you divide it among the larger it becomes. These will open to you the path which leads to eternity, and will raise you to a height from whence none shall cast you down.
source_reference: On the Shortness of Life, Section 15

plain_english: This is the only way to extend your mortal life — or even make it immortal. High office, monuments, everything that ambition records in decrees or builds in stone — it all fades away quickly. Time destroys everything. But the things that Philosophy has marked as its own cannot be harmed. No age will throw them out or weaken them. Each new century will respect them even more. We look at what's close to us with jealous, critical eyes. But we admire what's distant with less bias.
original_excerpt: By this means alone can you prolong your mortal life, nay, even turn it into an immortal one. High office, monuments, all that ambition records in decrees or piles up in stone, soon passes away: lapse of time casts down and ruins everything; but those things on which Philosophy has set its seal are beyond the reach of injury: no age will discard them or lessen their force, each succeeding century will add somewhat to the respect in which they are held: for we look upon what is near us with jealous eyes, but we admire what is further off with less prejudice.
source_reference: On the Shortness of Life, Section 15

plain_english: The wise person's life contains much more than most. They aren't trapped by the same limits that confine everyone else. They alone are free from the laws that govern ordinary people. All of history serves them like a god. If time has passed, they bring it back through memory. If time is present, they use it fully. If time is future, they prepare for it. Their life is long because they gather all times into it.
original_excerpt: The wise man's life, therefore, includes much: he is not hedged in by the same limits which confine others: he alone is exempt from the laws by which mankind is governed: all ages serve him like a god. If any time be past, he recals it by his memory; if it be present, he uses it; if it be future, he anticipates it: his life is a long one because he concentrates all times into it.
source_reference: On the Shortness of Life, Section 15
